stories.1: Isaac Watts wrote this as a song version of Psalm 90, the prayer of Moses. It was part of his book of the Psalms set to verse. In 1738, John Wesley changed the first words to “O God, our help.” Many hymnals still sing it Wesley’s way, but this book keeps Watts’s “Our God.”
stories.2: No one knows who first wrote this hymn in German. It was printed in 1828 in a hymnbook for the churches around Würzburg, a city in Germany, with fourteen short verses. Every verse ends with the same words of praise, which mean “May Jesus Christ be praised!” Edward Caswall, an Englishman, put it into English in the 1850s.
stories.3: This hymn was first printed in 1861 in a magazine called The Family Treasury. James Drummond Burns was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, and later led a church in Hampstead, near London. He also wrote the article on hymns for the Encyclopaedia Britannica.
stories.4: Reginald Heber wrote this hymn for Trinity Sunday while he was the pastor of a village church in Hodnet, England. He wanted hymns to fit each Sunday of the church year. Its words echo Revelation 4, where the creatures around God’s throne sing “Holy, holy, holy.” Heber later served as a bishop in India and died there in 1826. The hymn was printed after his death.
stories.5: Harriet Beecher Stowe, who wrote the novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin, wrote this hymn in 1853. It grew from Psalm 139:18: “When I awake, I am still with thee.” It was first printed in 1855 in a hymnbook put together by her brother, the preacher Henry Ward Beecher.
stories.14: This hymn first appeared in 1773 in a book of added hymns, with no writer’s name. Since 1786 it has often been credited to John Fawcett, an English pastor, but no one knows for sure. It was written to close a time of worship, before people go home.
stories.16: “Good-bye” began as a short way of saying “God be with you.” Jeremiah Rankin, a pastor in Washington, D.C., wanted to bring back that meaning. He wrote this hymn as a Christian good-bye, a blessing for friends when they part.
stories.18: Isaac Watts wrote this as a song version of Psalm 117, the shortest chapter in the Bible. The psalm has only two verses, so Watts wrote only two. It calls every land and every language to praise God. Later hymnbooks added more verses to make it longer.
stories.19: Fanny Crosby wrote the words to this hymn, and Chester Allen wrote the tune. It was first printed in 1869 in Bright Jewels, a songbook that Allen helped put together. Every verse begins with the same call: “Praise Him! Praise Him! Jesus, our blessed Redeemer!”
stories.20: No one knows who wrote this hymn. It was printed on a small leaflet in England by 1757. Its lines fit the tune of “God Save the King,” and at first people sang it to that tune. In 1769 Felice de Giardini wrote it a tune of its own.
stories.21: Robert Grant wrote this as a song version of Psalm 104, which praises God for the sky, the earth, and the sea. He drew on an older version of the same psalm, printed in 1561. Grant was born in India and later served in Britain’s Parliament.
stories.22: Frederick Faber first printed this in 1854 as a hymn of eight verses. It began, “Souls of men! why will ye scatter like a crowd of frightened sheep?” In 1862 he added five more verses. Many hymnbooks now begin with what was his fourth verse: “There’s a wideness in God’s mercy, like the wideness of the sea.”
stories.23: Henry Williams Baker wrote this song version of Psalm 23 for an English hymnbook, Hymns Ancient and Modern, which he helped put together. His friend John Ellerton said that Baker’s last words were from its third verse: “Perverse and foolish oft I strayed, but yet in love He sought me.”
stories.24: James Montgomery was born in Scotland and ran a newspaper in Sheffield, England, for many years. He wrote hundreds of hymns. This one is his song version of Psalm 23, from his book of psalms, Songs of Zion. He also wrote the Christmas hymn “Angels, from the Realms of Glory.”
stories.27: Mary Lathbury wrote this hymn beside Lake Chautauqua in New York, at a summer school for Bible study. Bishop John H. Vincent, who started the school, asked her for a song for its study classes. So it was written for people studying the Bible together, not for the Lord’s Supper. She wrote so many songs for the school that people called her its poet.
stories.28: Marcus Wells was a farmer near Hartwick, New York, who also made farm tools. He said the idea for this hymn came to him on a Saturday afternoon in October 1858, while he was at work in his cornfield. The next day he finished the words, wrote a tune for them, and sent them to Isaac Woodbury, who printed them that November in his music paper in New York.
stories.29: George Croly was born in Dublin, Ireland, and spent much of his life as a writer in London. Late in life he led a church in a poor part of London. He wanted new hymns for it, so he put together his own hymnbook and wrote some of the hymns himself. This hymn is from that book.
stories.30: Andrew Reed wrote this prayer to the Holy Spirit in 1817, the year he first put together a book of added hymns. He was a pastor in London. In 1813 he had started a home there for children who had lost their parents. Later he started more homes like it, and a hospital for people who could not be cured.
stories.31: Isaac Watts did not write this as a Christmas song. It is his take on Psalm 98, which calls the whole earth to sing for joy because the Lord is coming. It was part of his book of the Psalms set to verse. Over time, people began singing it at Christmas.
stories.32: Charles Wesley wrote this as a “Hymn for Christmas-Day” in 1739. His first line was “Hark, how all the welkin rings.” Welkin is an old word for the sky. In the 1750s another preacher, George Whitefield, changed it to “Hark! the herald angels sing” in his own hymnbook.
stories.33: This hymn first appeared as a poem on December 29, 1849, in the Christian Register, a church paper in Boston. Its writer, Edmund Sears, was the pastor of a small church in Wayland, Massachusetts. It speaks of the angels’ song of peace on earth.
stories.34: James Montgomery first printed this as a poem in his own newspaper, the Sheffield Iris, on Christmas Eve, 1816. He called it “The Nativity,” an old word for the birth of Jesus. It came into wide use in churches after it was printed again in 1825.
stories.35: In 1865 Phillips Brooks, a pastor from Philadelphia, traveled to the land where Jesus lived. On Christmas Eve he rode on horseback from Jerusalem to Bethlehem and went out to the field where the shepherds are said to have heard the angels. Three years later he wrote this poem for the children of his church’s Sunday school. He asked Lewis Redner, the church organist, to write music for it.
stories.36: This hymn was first written in Latin, as “Adeste Fideles.” The oldest copies, from the 1740s, are in the handwriting of John Francis Wade, an Englishman who copied church music and lived in France. He is often named as its writer, but no one knows for sure. In 1841 Frederick Oakeley, an English priest, put it into English. His first try began, “Ye faithful, approach ye.”
stories.37: Joseph Mohr, a young priest in Austria, wrote these words as a poem in 1816. Two years later he was serving at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf, a town near Salzburg. On Christmas Eve, 1818, he asked his friend Franz Gruber, a teacher and organist, to write a tune for it, with a part for guitar. That night the two of them sang it at the church for the first time, with Mohr playing the guitar.
stories.38: Josiah Holland wrote this Christmas poem in 1872. It did not appear in a church hymnbook until 1905, more than thirty years later. Holland trained as a doctor, but he became a writer and the editor of Scribner’s Monthly, a magazine.
stories.39: Theodore Williams was a pastor in New York City for many years. In 1899 he became the first head of Hackley School, a new school in Tarrytown, New York. He also put the poetry of Virgil, a writer of ancient Rome, into English. His wife, Velma, put together a hymnbook that included several of his hymns.
stories.40: This Christmas hymn was printed in 1868 in a new edition of The Rivulet, Thomas Toke Lynch’s book of hymns. Its first line counts the years since Jesus was born: “A thousand years have come and gone, and near a thousand more.” Lynch led small churches in London.
stories.41: This hymn was printed in the 1870s in songbooks for Sunday schools. It tells of the star the wise men followed to the young child Jesus (Matthew 2:9). Rossiter Raymond was a mining engineer in New York who also wrote hymns. He belonged to Plymouth Church in Brooklyn.
stories.42: Paul Gerhardt, a pastor in Germany, wrote this Christmas hymn in German, in fifteen verses. It was first printed in the 1650s in a hymnbook put together by the musician Johann Crüger. Its first line means “My heart shall leap for joy.” In 1858 Catherine Winkworth put part of it into English for her book of German hymns, Lyra Germanica.
stories.43: Godfrey Thring wrote this hymn in 1873 for Epiphany, the day in early January when many churches remember the wise men who followed the star to Jesus (Matthew 2). He wrote it to be sung as people walk in at the start of the service. It was first printed the next year in his book Hymns and Sacred Lyrics.
stories.44: No one knows who wrote this hymn. Its two verses were first printed in 1885, in a Sunday school book made by a Lutheran church in Philadelphia. Two years later, James Murray set it to his own tune and called it “Luther’s Cradle Hymn,” saying Martin Luther wrote it for his children. That was a mistake, but Luther’s name stayed on it for many years.
stories.45: John Bowring based this hymn on Isaiah 21:11, where a voice calls out in the dark, “Watchman, what of the night?” The hymn is a talk between a traveler and a watchman on the city wall. The traveler asks what signs the night holds, and the watchman points to a rising star that brings the day. It was printed in 1825 in Bowring’s book of hymns, the same book as “In the Cross of Christ I Glory.” Churches often sing it in the weeks before Christmas.
stories.46: Reginald Heber wrote this for Epiphany, the day in early January when churches remember the wise men who followed a star to the baby Jesus (Matthew 2:1–11). It was first printed in November 1811 in a magazine, the Christian Observer, signed only “D.R.,” the last letters of his first and last names. Its verses ask what gift to bring Him and answer, “Dearer to God are the prayers of the poor.” It was not put in a hymnbook until after his death.
stories.47: William Chatterton Dix wrote this on Epiphany, January 6, the day churches remember the wise men. He was sick in bed at his home in Bristol, England, and could not go to church. He read that day’s Bible reading, the story of the wise men in Matthew 2, and by evening he had finished the hymn. He also wrote “What Child Is This?”
stories.48: Folliott Pierpoint was born in Bath, England. He is said to have written this hymn after looking out over the hills around the city on a spring day. He first wrote it for the Lord’s Supper, in eight verses, and it was printed in 1864 in a book of hymns for that service. Its chorus first said, “Christ, our God, to Thee we raise this our sacrifice of praise.” Later books changed the chorus so it could be sung at any time.
stories.49: William Channing Gannett was the minister of a church in St. Paul, Minnesota. In 1882 he wrote this for the children of its Sunday school, and called it “Mary’s Manger Song.” In it, Mary sings her newborn to sleep in the hay. In the second verse she wonders what lies ahead for Him. It was printed in 1894 in a book of hymns and poems, The Thought of God, which Gannett made with Frederick Hosmer.
stories.50: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote this poem, “Christmas Bells,” on a Christmas Day during the American Civil War. In late 1863 his son Charles, a young soldier, was badly wounded in battle, but lived. In the poem he hears the bells and says, “There is no peace on earth,” until they ring louder: “God is not dead, nor doth he sleep.” It was first printed in February 1865 in Our Young Folks, a magazine for children. Its two verses about the war are left out of most hymnbooks, this one too.
stories.51: James Blaisdell grew up in Beloit, Wisconsin, and became a pastor. Later he taught the Bible at Beloit College, and in 1910 he became the president of Pomona College in California. His hymn finds the wise men’s gifts in everyday kindness. Sharing someone’s sorrow brings frankincense to Jesus, and caring for “the least of them” brings Him gold. It echoes Matthew 25:40, where Jesus says that what we do for “the least of these,” we do for Him.
stories.52: In 1841 Jemima Luke heard a Greek marching tune at a school for young children in London. Later, riding alone in a stagecoach, she wrote the first two verses in pencil on the back of an old envelope, so the children at a village school she visited could sing that tune. It tells of Jesus calling the little children to Him (Mark 10:14). Her father sent it to a Sunday school magazine without telling her, and it was printed that same year.
stories.53: H. R. Palmer asked Mary Ann Baker for songs to go with that year’s Sunday school lessons. One lesson was the story of Jesus calming the storm (Mark 4:35–41). Not long before, her brother had died of a lung disease far from home. She later said the storm she wrote about was the one in her own heart, and that Jesus’ voice brought it to calm. Palmer wrote the tune.
stories.54: William Walsham How wrote this after reading “Brothers, and a Sermon,” a poem by Jean Ingelow. The poem is built on Revelation 3:20, where Jesus says, “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.” How said he read its lines over and over, then closed the book and wrote his first try on an old scrap of paper. It was printed in 1867 in a hymnbook he helped put together.
stories.55: Theodulph was a bishop in Orléans, France, and a poet at the court of the emperor Charlemagne. Around 820, while he was held in prison in the city of Angers, he wrote this hymn in Latin for Palm Sunday, the day the crowds praised Jesus as He rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:1–11). It was written for people to sing as they walked into church on that day, and churches still sing it then. In the 1850s John Mason Neale put it into English.
stories.56: This began as a French song for a solo singer, “Les Rameaux,” which means “The Palms.” It was printed in Paris in 1864. Jean-Baptiste Faure, a famous singer at the Paris Opera, wrote the music, and Jules Bertrand wrote the French words. It tells of the crowds who spread palm branches in Jesus’ path as He came into Jerusalem (John 12:12–13). Several people later made English versions of it.
stories.57: No one knows who wrote this hymn. It was first printed in German in 1677, in a hymnbook from the city of Münster. The English words most people sing first appeared in 1850, in a collection by Richard Storrs Willis. The translator’s name was not given.
stories.58: Cecil Frances Alexander wrote a book of hymns for children, to help them understand the Apostles’ Creed, an old statement of what Christians believe. Each hymn explains a line of it. This one explains “suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead, and buried.” The book was printed in 1848, while she lived in Strabane, a town in Ireland. Money from the book went to a school for deaf children.
stories.59: Elizabeth Clephane lived most of her life in Melrose, a town in Scotland. She wrote this hymn about a year before she died, at 38. Three years after her death, a Scottish magazine printed it with other poems of hers, without her name.
stories.60: Isaac Watts wrote this to be sung at the Lord’s Supper. He based it on Galatians 6:14, where Paul says he will boast only in the cross of Jesus. Charles Wesley, who wrote thousands of hymns himself, is said to have called it better than any of his own.
stories.61: John Bowring based this hymn on Galatians 6:14, where Paul says he will boast only in the cross of Jesus. It is the same verse behind “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross.” It was printed in 1825 in his book of hymns. When he died in 1872, its first line was carved on his gravestone.
stories.62: John of Damascus was born in Damascus and later became a monk at Mar Saba, a monastery near Jerusalem. Around 750 he wrote a long Easter hymn in Greek, and these words come from its first part. In Greek churches it was sung just after midnight on Easter morning, as candles were lit and people called out, “Christ is risen!” In 1862 John Mason Neale put it into English.
stories.63: Charles Wesley wrote this as a “Hymn for Easter Day,” with eleven verses. It was first sung at the Foundery, the first meeting house he and his brother John opened in London. Many hymnals add “Alleluia!” after each line. Wesley didn’t write those. Someone added them later so the words would fit a well-known Easter tune.
stories.64: This Easter hymn was first printed in 1769, in a hymnbook made for Baptist churches in Bristol, England. Thomas Scott, from Norwich, wrote it. Some years later another writer, Thomas Gibbons, changed some lines and added verses. Since then books have mixed up who wrote it, and many, this one too, name them both.
stories.65: Matthew Bridges wrote this hymn about Jesus going up into heaven, forty days after Easter (Acts 1:3, 9). It pictures Him passing through heaven’s “gates of gold” to take His crown. It was printed in his book Hymns of the Heart. Bridges also wrote “Crown Him with Many Crowns,” and late in life he lived for some years in Quebec, Canada.
stories.66: Thomas Kelly, an Irish hymn writer, set this hymn under Revelation 11:15: “And he shall reign for ever and ever.” It pictures Jesus, once mocked as the Man of Sorrows (Isaiah 53:3), now crowned in heaven. It was printed in 1809 in the third edition of his book Hymns on Various Passages of Scripture.
stories.67: This hymn first came out in pieces, with no writer’s name. Its first verse was printed in November 1779 in the Gospel Magazine, edited by Augustus Toplady, who wrote “Rock of Ages.” The whole hymn, eight verses called “On the Resurrection, the Lord Is King,” followed in April 1780. A few years later it was printed again in a little book that also held a poem whose first letters spell “Edward Perronet.”
stories.68: Matthew Bridges based this hymn on Revelation 19:12, where John sees Jesus with “many crowns” on His head. He printed it in 1851, in six verses, in a new edition of his book Hymns of the Heart. In 1874 Godfrey Thring, an English pastor, wrote six verses of his own that begin the same way. Many hymnbooks now mix verses from both.
stories.69: Samuel Medley joined Britain’s navy as a teenager. In 1759 he was badly hurt in a sea battle off the coast of Portugal and had to leave. While he was healing, someone read him a sermon by Isaac Watts, and it turned him toward God. He became a pastor and spent his last 27 years leading a church in Liverpool, a busy port, where he worked among the sailors. He wrote more than 200 hymns.
stories.70: This hymn first appeared in 1757, as two verses in a small hymnbook printed with no writers’ names. It is often credited to John Bakewell, but no one knows for sure how much of it he wrote. In 1760 Martin Madan added more lines in his own hymnbook, and in 1776 Augustus Toplady changed a few more. This book’s version holds lines from all three.
stories.71: Charles Wesley shaped this hymn on a popular song of his day, “Fairest Isle, All Isles Excelling,” from an opera about King Arthur. That song praises Britain as the finest island of all. Wesley kept its sound and shape but turned it into a prayer that God’s love would come and live in our hearts: “Fix in us Thy humble dwelling.” It was first printed in 1747 in a small book of his hymns.
stories.72: Katherine Hankey wrote a long poem about Jesus in 1866, while she was getting well from a serious illness in London. It had fifty verses in two parts, “The Story Wanted” and “The Story Told.” This hymn comes from the first part, and “I Love to Tell the Story” comes from the second. In 1867 the composer William Doane heard the poem read aloud at a large YMCA meeting in Montreal, Canada, and later set it to music.
stories.73: Elizabeth Codner wrote this in the summer of 1860, after news came from Ireland that many people there were turning to God. In it she asks God to bless her too, and each verse ends with the words “Even me.” She headed it with words from Genesis 27:38: “Bless me, even me also, O my father.”
stories.74: Little is known about E. W. Blandy, who wrote these words. The hymn was printed in 1890, with a tune by John S. Norris. Hymn histories say Blandy, an officer in the Salvation Army, wrote it after he chose to serve in a poor, crowded part of New York City instead of at a settled church. Its first verse echoes Jesus’ call in Mark 8:34 to “take up his cross, and follow me.”
stories.75: Gerhard Tersteegen wrote this in German, as “Gott rufet noch,” for his book of hymns and poems, Spiritual Flower Garden. Its English words were first printed in 1855 in Hymns from the Land of Luther, a book of German hymns put into English by two sisters from Scotland, Jane Borthwick and Sarah Findlater. This hymnal names Jane as the translator. But Jane later helped sort out which hymns in their book were hers, and this one was Sarah’s.
stories.76: Charlotte Elliott lived in Brighton, England, with her brother Henry, a pastor. He was raising money to open a school there, St. Mary’s Hall, for the daughters of pastors. One day the family went to a sale to raise money for the school, but Charlotte was too ill to go. At home alone, she wrote this hymn. Years before, a visiting preacher, César Malan, had told her she could come to Jesus just as she was.
stories.77: Horatius Bonar was a pastor in Kelso, a town in Scotland. He saw that the children in his church understood little of the old psalms they sang, so he began writing simple hymns for them. He first called this one “The Voice from Galilee.” Each verse begins with words Jesus said in the Gospels, then answers them.
stories.77b: Matthew Bridges wrote this for confirmation, a church service where people say for themselves that they will follow Jesus. He called it “Confirmation” and printed it in 1848, in five verses, in his book Hymns of the Heart. Its first verse asks God to keep the singer from straying, much like Psalm 119:10: “O let me not wander from thy commandments.”
stories.78: Thomas Moore, an Irish poet, printed this in 1816 in his book Sacred Songs. He wrote many of the songs in it to fit well-known tunes from other lands. In 1831 Thomas Hastings, an American church musician, changed some of its lines and wrote a new third verse. Moore’s “Come, at the shrine of God” became Hastings’s “Come to the mercy seat,” a Bible name for the place where God meets His people. Most books, this one too, sing it Hastings’s way.
stories.80: Cecil Frances Alexander wrote this for St. Andrew’s Day, November 30, when many churches remember Andrew, one of Jesus’ first followers. The Bible reading for that day tells how Jesus called Andrew and his brother Peter away from their fishing nets (Matthew 4:18–20). Her husband, a pastor, is said to have asked her for verses to go with his sermon that day. It was printed in 1852 in a hymnbook made in England.
stories.81: William Sleeper was a pastor in Worcester, Massachusetts, for about thirty years. He sent these words to George Stebbins, who led the singing at D. L. Moody’s meetings, and Stebbins wrote the tune. It was printed in 1887. Each line leaves one thing behind and comes to another: out of sorrow and into gladness, out of sickness and into health.
stories.82: Charles Wesley printed this in 1742, in five verses, in a book of hymns by him and his brother John. He set it under the words “Behold the Man!” Pilate said that when he brought Jesus out wearing the crown of thorns (John 19:5). Later the hymn looks to Jesus in heaven, who speaks to God for us (Romans 8:34).
stories.83: Hugh Stowell was born on the Isle of Man, an island between England and Ireland, and became a pastor in England. This hymn was first printed in 1828 in The Winter’s Wreath, a yearly book of new poems and stories. He called it “The Mercy Seat,” and every verse ends with those words. In the Bible the mercy seat was the gold cover of the ark of the covenant, where God promised to meet with His people (Exodus 25:22). A few years later he rewrote the hymn for his own hymnbook.
stories.84: William Hammond printed this in 1745 in his book Psalms, Hymns, and Spiritual Songs. It is a prayer for the start of a worship service. He first wrote it long, eight verses of eight lines each. In 1760 Martin Madan cut it down to six short verses for his own hymnbook, and most books since have used that shorter form.
stories.85: This hymn first appeared on the front page of the New York Observer, a newspaper, on September 13, 1845. A pastor named Thomas Salmon sent it in. He wrote that in Coleshill, a town in England, he had known a blind preacher named W. W. Walford, who said the poem aloud while Salmon copied it down in pencil. No one has been able to find out for sure who that man was. William Bradbury wrote the tune it is sung to in 1861.
stories.86: This hymn was printed in 1891 under the name Charles Bruce. That was one of the many other names Fanny Crosby wrote under. She wrote so many hymns that publishers did not want her own name to fill their books. Ira Sankey wrote its tune. Its chorus, “Send showers of blessing,” echoes Ezekiel 34:26: “there shall be showers of blessing.”
stories.87: Sarah Flower Adams’s pastor, William Johnson Fox, was preparing a sermon on Jacob’s dream of a ladder reaching to heaven (Genesis 28). He asked her for a hymn to go with it. Her sister Eliza, a composer, wrote its first tune.
stories.88: Sybil Partridge was a Catholic sister in Liverpool, England, where she took the name Sister Mary Xavier. The sisters there ran a college that trained young women to be teachers. She wrote most of her verses for its students, and years later she gathered them into a book that she gave to them. This prayer asks for God’s help just for today and leaves tomorrow in His hands.
stories.89: In 1872 Annie Hawks lived in Brooklyn, New York. One day, busy with her housework, she felt how near God was, and the words “I need thee every hour” came into her mind. She gave the verses to her pastor, Robert Lowry, who wrote the tune and added the chorus. It was first sung that November at a large Sunday school meeting in Cincinnati, Ohio. Years later, after her husband died, she wrote that only then did she understand the comfort in its words.
stories.90: Charles Wesley wrote this within two years of 1738, the year he came to a new trust in Jesus. It was printed in 1740, in five verses, in a book of hymns by him and his brother John. He headed it “In Temptation,” a prayer for the times when doing wrong pulls hard at us. In the hymn that struggle is a storm at sea, and Jesus is the safe harbor.
stories.91: Augustus Toplady first printed four lines of this in 1775, inside a magazine article. The whole hymn came out in March 1776, in the Gospel Magazine, which he edited at the time. The words “Rock of Ages” come from Isaiah 26:4, where the Hebrew calls God an “everlasting rock.” “Cleft” means split open. The hymn joins Moses, kept safe in a cleft of the rock while God passed by (Exodus 33:22), to Jesus, whose side was pierced on the cross (John 19:34).
stories.92: Frances Ridley Havergal wrote this in September 1874, while staying at Ormont Dessous, a village in Switzerland. She called it “Trusting Jesus.” It was first printed on a small sheet of paper, and in 1878 in her book Loyal Responses, in six verses. It is said to have been her favorite of her own hymns, and a copy was found in her Bible after she died.
stories.93: Isabella Stevenson was born in Cheltenham, England, in 1843. She wrote this prayer for loved ones far away for a private reason of her own, and it is the only hymn of hers that is known. It was printed in 1889 in an added section of Hymns Ancient and Modern, an English hymnbook. Many later books placed it among hymns for travelers and absent friends.
stories.94: In August 1875 Edward Bickersteth was on holiday in Harrogate, a town in England. On Sunday he heard the town’s pastor preach on Isaiah 26:3: “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.” The pastor said that in Hebrew the verse says “peace, peace,” and that this means perfect peace. That afternoon Bickersteth visited an old relative who was dying. He wrote this hymn there and read it to him.
stories.95: William Williams was a traveling preacher in Wales. This hymn of his was first printed in Welsh in 1762, and its first line means “Lord, lead me through the wilderness.” In 1771 Peter Williams, no relation, put some of its verses into English, and the next year William made English verses of his own. Its pictures come from Israel’s journey through the desert: bread from heaven (Exodus 16), water from the rock (Exodus 17), and the pillar of fire and cloud (Exodus 13:21–22).
stories.96: John Henry Newman fell very ill with a fever while traveling in Sicily, far from his home in England. When he was well enough, he found a place on a boat carrying oranges to France. The wind died, and the boat sat still for a week between the islands of Corsica and Sardinia. He wrote this prayer there.
stories.97: William Cushing was a pastor for more than twenty years. After his wife died in 1870, poor health made him leave his church, and he turned to writing hymns. He said this one grew out of “many tears” and many struggles of his own. Ira Sankey wrote its tune. Its first line echoes Psalm 61:2: “lead me to the rock that is higher than I.”
stories.98: Edward Hopper was the pastor of the Church of Sea and Land, near the harbor in New York City, where many sailors came. He wrote this hymn for them, in words they knew: chart, compass, and a pilot to steer the ship. It was printed in 1871 in The Sailors’ Magazine, put out by a group that helped sailors. John Gould wrote its tune the same year.
stories.99: On March 26, 1862, Joseph Gilmore spoke at a midweek service at a church in Philadelphia. He meant to explain Psalm 23, but he got no further than the words “He leadeth me.” Afterward, at his host’s home, he wrote this hymn in pencil and handed it to his wife. Without telling him, she sent it to a Boston paper, the Watchman and Reflector, which printed it in December. In 1865 he found it in a hymnbook, set to a tune by William Bradbury.
stories.100: This hymn comes from a long Latin poem about Jesus, written in the 1100s. For hundreds of years people said that Bernard of Clairvaux, a famous monk in France, wrote it. Scholars now think it was more likely written by a monk in England whose name is lost. In 1858 Ray Palmer, who also wrote “My Faith Looks Up to Thee,” chose five of its verses and made this English hymn from them, freely rather than word for word. It was first printed that year in The Sabbath Hymn Book.
stories.101: Henry Burton was born in Swannington, England, in 1840. When he was young, his family moved to Wisconsin, where he went to Beloit College and began to preach. He then went back to England, and from 1865 he served there as a Methodist pastor, mostly in Lancashire and London. This hymn is a prayer for people far out at sea, who find God near “on the wide ocean.” Hymnbooks of its time set it among hymns for travelers and for those at sea.
stories.103: This hymn comes from the same long Latin poem as “Jesus, Thou Joy of Loving Hearts,” and, like it, was long said to be by Bernard of Clairvaux. Edward Caswall, an English priest, put it into English. His version was first printed in a book of his in 1849, and he made it longer in a later book. Hymnbooks sing only a few of its verses. The first says that even the thought of Jesus fills the heart with sweetness, and that seeing His face will be sweeter still.
stories.104: John Greenleaf Whittier, an American poet, wrote a long poem called “Our Master” in 1866. Hymnbooks took a few of its verses to make this hymn, and other books chose other verses from it. The last verse this book sings begins with the poem’s own name for Jesus: “O Lord, and Master of us all.”
stories.105: Ozora Davis was a pastor in Vermont, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. In 1909, the year he wrote this hymn, he became the head of Chicago Theological Seminary, a school for pastors, and he led it for twenty years. The hymn finds Jesus beside us at work, “through din of market, whirl of wheels.” It also says that the hopes and tasks we know were His “in Galilee.”
stories.106: Joseph Scriven was born in Ireland and later moved to Canada. Around 1855 he wrote this poem to comfort his mother back in Ireland, who was going through a hard time, and sent it to her. He did not mean for anyone else to see it. For years even his close friends did not know he had written it. When asked, he is said to have answered, “The Lord and I did it between us.”
stories.107: Katherine Hankey wrote a long poem about Jesus in 1866, in two parts. The first part became the hymn “Tell Me the Old, Old Story.” This hymn comes from the second part, “The Story Told,” which she finished on November 18, 1866. In 1869 William Fischer wrote its tune and added a chorus.
stories.108: Sylvanus Dryden Phelps, a pastor in Connecticut, wrote this in 1862. It was first printed the next year, without his name, in The Youth’s Companion, a magazine in Boston, under the title “Something for Thee.” Robert Lowry later wrote its tune and printed it in his songbook Pure Gold. Every verse ends with the same three words, “Something for Thee.”
stories.110: George Matheson was a pastor in Innellan, a village on the coast of Scotland, and he was blind. He wrote this hymn there on the evening of June 6, 1882, the night of his sister’s wedding, when he was alone in the house. He said that something had happened to him that night, known only to himself, that caused him great pain of heart. He also said the hymn came to him in about five minutes, and that he never changed a word of it.
stories.111: No one knows for sure who wrote this hymn. It appeared without a name in Hymns for the Young, a book of hymns for children that Dorothy Thrupp put together. That is why it is often credited to her.
stories.112: Robert Robinson was 22 when he wrote this hymn. The word “Ebenezer” in it comes from 1 Samuel 7:12. After God helped Israel, Samuel set up a stone and named it Ebenezer, which means “stone of help.” He said, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.”
stories.113: Joseph Grigg printed this hymn in 1765 in a small book, Four Hymns on Divine Subjects. A magazine that printed it in 1774 said it was written “by a youth of ten years.” In 1787 Benjamin Francis changed many of its lines for John Rippon’s hymnbook, and many later books sing it his way. Its question, whether anyone could be ashamed of Jesus, echoes Jesus’ own words in Mark 8:38.
stories.114: Benjamin Schmolck grew up in Silesia, a land now part of Poland, where his father was a Lutheran pastor. He wrote this hymn in German around 1704, and its first line means just what the English says: “My Jesus, as Thou wilt.” It echoes Jesus’ prayer in the garden: “not what I will, but what thou wilt” (Mark 14:36). Jane Borthwick of Edinburgh, Scotland, put it into English. She and her sister, Sarah Findlater, made a book of German hymns in English, Hymns from the Land of Luther.
stories.115: Ray Palmer wrote this poem just after finishing college, while teaching at a girls’ school in New York. He kept it in a small notebook. Two years later he met the musician Lowell Mason in Boston, who was looking for new hymns. Mason copied it down and wrote a tune for it called Olivet. He told Palmer he would be remembered most for this hymn.
stories.116: Frances Ridley Havergal wrote this hymn late one night during a five-day visit to Areley House, a home in Worcestershire, England. She first wrote it as eleven short verses of two lines each. Her father, William Havergal, wrote one of the tunes it is sung to, called Patmos.
stories.119: James Montgomery wrote this prayer on October 13, 1834. On his first copy he wrote the names of 22 friends he sent copies to, and the date he sent each one. It was printed in his book Original Hymns in 1853. Later Frances Hutton, an Englishwoman, changed some of its lines, and many hymnbooks sing her version.
stories.122: This hymn was first printed in London in 1787, in a hymnbook made by John Rippon, a Baptist pastor. Where the writer’s name should be, the book printed only the letter “K.” The most likely writer is Robert Keene, who led the singing at Rippon’s church, but no one knows for sure. Rippon titled it “Exceeding great and precious promises,” words from 2 Peter 1:4. Its verses are built from God’s promises in the Bible, such as “Fear thou not; for I am with thee” (Isaiah 41:10).
stories.126: Norman Macleod was a pastor in Scotland. This hymn first appeared as a poem in 1857, in a church magazine in Edinburgh that he edited. Every verse comes back to one plain rule: “Trust in God, and do the right.” Arthur Sullivan later wrote the tune this book uses.
stories.136: Frances Ridley Havergal wrote this hymn at Winterdyne, her sister’s family home in Bewdley, England. She called it “A Worker’s Prayer” and set it under Romans 14:7: “For none of us liveth to himself.” She wrote it for people who help in their church.
stories.137: Theodore Chickering Williams was the pastor of All Souls Church in New York City for thirteen years. His wife, Velma Williams, made a hymnbook in 1890 and put several of his hymns in it. In 1899 he became the first head of the Hackley School, a new school in Tarrytown, New York. This hymn asks that every gift be shared with others: joy, harvest, strength, and the weight of sorrow. Its last line says that when the heart takes in a brother, “God is there.”
stories.139: D. L. Moody, a preacher, told of a ship coming into the harbor at Cleveland, Ohio, on a stormy night. The big lighthouse was shining, but the lower lights along the shore that marked the channel had gone out, and the ship missed its way and broke on the rocks. Moody ended, “the Master will take care of the great lighthouse: let us keep the lower lights burning!” Philip Bliss, who led the music at Moody’s meetings, wrote this hymn from that story. He wrote both the words and the tune.
stories.141: William Whiting taught the boys of a choir school in Winchester, England. One of his students was about to sail to the United States and was afraid of the voyage. Whiting wrote this hymn for him, drawing on Psalm 107, which tells of sailors God brings safely through a storm. In 1879 the U.S. Naval Academy began closing its Sunday services with it, and it became known as the Navy Hymn.
stories.142: Washington Gladden was a pastor who also edited a magazine called Sunday Afternoon. In March 1879 he printed this poem there, in a corner of the magazine called “The Still Hour,” with the title “Walking with God.” A year later Charles Richards found it and put it in his hymnbook, leaving out one of its three long verses. Hymnbooks since have sung it in the shorter form.
stories.145: Frank Mason North was born in New York City and worked for a Methodist group that served people in the city. Caleb Winchester, who was helping to make a new Methodist hymnbook, asked him to write a hymn for that work. Not long before, North had preached on Matthew 22:9, where the king in Jesus’ story sends his servants into the highways to invite everyone they find to the wedding feast. He printed the hymn in June 1903 in The Christian City, a magazine he edited, and called it “A Prayer for the Multitudes.”
stories.167: Psalm 72 is a prayer for the king, long linked with King Solomon. Isaac Watts made this hymn from the second half of that psalm, in his 1719 book of the Psalms set to verse. He wanted the psalms to speak as David would have spoken “had he lived in the days of Christianity.” So where the psalm prays for an earthly king, his first line names Jesus.
stories.169: This hymn was first printed in 1891 in The New Song, a Chicago songbook for Sunday schools, under the title “Go, Stand and Speak.” Mary Brown, a teacher in Jewett City, Connecticut, wrote the words, and Charles Prior wrote its first tune. Some hymnbooks say Prior also wrote its second and third verses. In 1894 Carrie Rounsefell wrote a new tune for it, and its chorus, “I’ll go where you want me to go, dear Lord,” became its best-known line.
stories.170: John Fawcett was the pastor of a small, poor church at Wainsgate, a village in Yorkshire, England. A large church in London asked him to come and be its pastor, and he said yes. The story is told that his good-bye sermon was preached and his wagons were loaded when his people’s tears changed his mind, and he stayed. This hymn is said to have come from that choice. It was first printed in 1782 in his own book of hymns, under the title “Brotherly Love.”
stories.171: Reginald Heber wrote this short prayer to be sung before the Lord’s Supper. In his book it carries just that heading: “Before the Sacrament.” It has only two verses, and its first words echo John 6, where Jesus calls Himself the living bread that gives life to the world. It was first printed in 1827, the year after Heber died, in his book of hymns for each Sunday of the church year.
stories.172: William Bright taught church history at Oxford University in England. He first printed this as a longer poem in October 1873, in a church magazine called The Monthly Packet. In 1875 the makers of the hymnbook Hymns Ancient and Modern left out its first two verses and changed one line, so that it began “And now, O Father, mindful of the love.” That shorter form is the one hymnbooks have sung ever since. It is a prayer for the Lord’s Supper.
stories.173: Psalm 137 is a song of God’s people far from home, by the rivers of Babylon, who promise never to forget Jerusalem. Timothy Dwight, the head of Yale College in Connecticut, made this hymn from its first six verses. He wrote it for his new edition of Isaac Watts’s book of psalms and titled it “Love to the Church.” Where the psalm longs for a city, the hymn turns that love toward God’s people.
stories.174: Thomas Pollock, an English pastor, wrote many hymns in the form of a litany: a prayer in many short parts, each answered with the same words. Here the answer is “We beseech thee, hear us.” A church group asked him for this one for a day of prayer in 1871, and he printed it that year. In 1875 he reworked it for the hymnbook Hymns Ancient and Modern, where it was called “Litany of the Church.” Each verse asks one thing for the church, such as that it be kept pure and patient.
stories.175: John Newton was a pastor in Olney, a small town in England. He and his friend, the poet William Cowper, wrote a book of hymns together, Olney Hymns. This one begins with Psalm 87:3: “Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God.” Years before, Newton had been the captain of ships that carried enslaved Africans. Later he wrote about the cruelty he had seen and his own part in it, and he worked to end Britain’s slave trade.
stories.176: Samuel Stone was a young assistant pastor in Windsor, England. He found that many poor people in his parish said the Apostles’ Creed in their prayers, an old summary of what Christians believe, without really understanding it. So in 1866 he wrote twelve hymns, one for each part of the Creed. This one is for the part that says “the holy catholic church, the communion of saints,” where “catholic” means the whole church everywhere. Its first lines build on 1 Corinthians 3:11: “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.”
stories.178: Henry Alford, an English pastor and Bible scholar, wrote this in 1844 for the harvest festival, when English churches gave thanks for the crops brought in. He titled it “After Harvest.” Its later verses turn to Jesus’ story of the wheat and the weeds, which grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24–30). So the hymn thanks God for this year’s crops and looks ahead to God’s last harvest.
stories.179: No one knows who first wrote this hymn. Its oldest English form is a long poem copied by hand in the late 1500s or early 1600s and signed only with the letters “F.B.P.” It grew from an old Latin prayer about the heavenly Jerusalem, a prayer long but wrongly said to be by Augustine. In Scotland, a version beginning “O Mother dear, Jerusalem” was long credited to David Dickson, a pastor who taught at the university in Glasgow.
stories.180: Bernard was a monk at Cluny, a great abbey in France, in the 1100s. Around 1145 he wrote a Latin poem almost 3,000 lines long. Most of it is about the wrongs of the world in his day, but parts of it picture heaven and its peace. In 1849 Richard Trench printed parts of the poem, and the English hymn writer John Mason Neale later put them into English. Several hymns came from Neale’s English version, and this is one of them.
stories.181: Henry Alford was the head of Canterbury Cathedral in England when he wrote this hymn. He printed its first three verses in March 1867 in a magazine called Good Words, and later that year in The Year of Praise, a hymnbook he made for the cathedral. He added a fourth verse in 1870. Its first line comes from Revelation 5:11, where John hears the voices of the angels around God’s throne, “ten thousand times ten thousand.”
stories.185: John Cennick was born in Reading, England, and became a traveling preacher who worked with John Wesley and George Whitefield. In 1742 he printed this hymn in a book called Sacred Hymns for the Children of God in the Days of Their Pilgrimage. He titled it “Encouragement to Praise,” and at first it had twelve verses. It pictures God’s people as travelers on their way home to God, singing as they go.
stories.190: Maxwell Cornelius grew up on a farm in Pennsylvania and became a bricklayer and builder in Pittsburgh. After he was badly hurt while building a house, he went to college and became a pastor, and later he led a church in Pasadena, California. When his wife died, he preached at her funeral himself, and he quoted this poem, which he had written not long before. A newspaper printed the sermon and the poem, and Daniel Whittle found it there and carried it in his Bible for three months before he added a chorus. Whittle’s friend James McGranahan wrote the tune.
stories.191: Robert Lowry was the pastor of Hanson Place Baptist Church in Brooklyn, New York. One very hot afternoon in July 1864, worn out by the heat, he began to think about the river in Revelation 22:1, the “pure river of water of life” flowing from God’s throne. The hymn came to him as a question and an answer: “Shall we gather at the river?” and then “Yes, we’ll gather.” He wrote the tune along with the words. It was first printed the next year in his songbook Happy Voices.
stories.192: Its first verse sets God’s words in Isaiah 1:18 to music, almost word for word: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.” In Isaiah that promise begins with an invitation: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD.” Fanny Crosby wrote the words around it, and William Doane wrote the tune. Her second verse turns it into a call to come home: “O return ye unto God!”
stories.193: Fanny Crosby wrote the words and George Stebbins wrote the tune. It was first printed in 1883 in Gospel Hymns No. 4, a songbook of its day. Years later Stebbins wrote that nothing special happened to lead either of them to write it. Its verses hear Jesus calling the weary to rest and asking anyone with a burden to bring it to Him.
stories.194: This was one of the first hymns Fanny Crosby wrote with the composer William Doane. In 1868 he gave her its first line as the subject for a hymn. That same year she spoke at a service in a prison in New York City and heard a man cry out, “Good Lord, do not pass me by.” Its words echo the blind man by the road near Jericho, who called out to Jesus as He passed (Luke 18:35–43).
stories.195: Fanny Crosby was staying with the composer William Doane at his home in Cincinnati, Ohio. One evening, as the sun went down, they talked together about how near God is. Before she went to sleep that night, the words of this hymn were in her mind, and the next morning she said them to Doane, who wrote them down and made the tune. It was first printed in 1875 with a verse from Hebrews 10:22 under it: “Let us draw near with a true heart.”
stories.196: Ellen Knight Bradford wrote this hymn, and E. H. Phelps wrote its tune. It was first printed in 1878 in Gospel Hymns No. 3, under the title “Over the Line.” In it Jesus calls a person to take just one step toward Him. To the worry that her sins are many and her faith is small, the answer comes that she need not trust in herself at all.
stories.197: William Cowper was an English poet and a friend of John Newton, the pastor who wrote “Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken.” This hymn was first printed in 1772, without his name, in a hymnbook made by Richard Conyers. Seven years later Cowper and Newton printed it again in their book, Olney Hymns, under the heading “Praise for the fountain opened.” The heading points to Zechariah 13:1, which promises a fountain that will wash away sin.
stories.198: Elisha Hoffman was a pastor in Ohio, Michigan, and Illinois, and he wrote more than 2,000 hymns. He wrote both the words and the tune of this one. It was first printed in 1891 in Gospel Hymns No. 6, a songbook of its day. In every verse, each line is answered by the same glad cry: “What a wonderful Saviour!”
stories.200: Fanny Crosby lost her sight as a baby and went on to write thousands of hymns. For this one, the tune came first. William Doane wrote the music, and she wrote words to fit it. It was first printed in a book of songs for Sunday schools.
stories.202: Francis Rowley was the pastor of First Baptist Church in North Adams, Massachusetts. In 1886, during weeks of special meetings at the church, a young musician named Peter Bilhorn led the singing. Bilhorn asked him to write a hymn he could set to music, and Rowley wrote the words that night. They began as a question: “Can’t you sing the wondrous story?” Ira Sankey changed the first words to “I will sing” when he printed it in 1887 with Bilhorn’s tune.
stories.203: Lewis Hartsough was the pastor of the Methodist church in Epworth, Iowa. He wrote both the words and the tune during special meetings at his church in 1872. That year he printed it in The Revivalist, a songbook he helped make. The next year Ira Sankey came across it, and it was soon sung at meetings in England and America. In Wales it became a well-loved hymn in Welsh, “Gwahoddiad,” which means “invitation.”
stories.204: Girolamo Savonarola was a friar, a brother in a Christian religious order, who preached in Florence, Italy, in the late 1400s. He wrote hymns and poems in Italian. Some of them were printed in 1563, in a book of Italian songs of praise. In 1853 Jane Francesca Wilde, a poet from Ireland, put this one into English for a book about his life. Its verses look at Jesus on the cross and ask for hearts that love Him more.
stories.205: Will Thompson grew up in East Liverpool, Ohio, and studied music in Boston. When music publishers turned down his songs, he started his own company to print them. He wrote both the words and the tune of this hymn, and it was first printed in 1879. He also wrote “Softly and Tenderly Jesus Is Calling.”
stories.206: Fanny Crosby wrote these words and gave them to Robert Lowry, the pastor who wrote “Shall We Gather at the River.” He wrote the tune for her words. It was first printed in 1875 in Brightest and Best, a songbook for Sunday schools that Lowry made with William Doane, under the heading “Jesus the Guide.” Its first line echoes Deuteronomy 32:12: “So the LORD alone did lead him.”
stories.207: William Cushing wrote this hymn late in his life, in 1896. Ira Sankey wrote the tune and printed it that same year in his songbook Sacred Songs No. 1. Its words come from Psalm 91:4: “He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust.” They also echo a prayer in Psalm 17:8: “hide me under the shadow of thy wings.” Cushing also wrote “O Safe to the Rock That Is Higher Than I.”
stories.208: The name printed with this hymn, Charlotte G. Homer, was a pen name of Charles Gabriel, who wrote many gospel songs. When he wrote both the words and the tune, he often signed the words with that name. This one was first printed in 1905. Its refrain says, “From sinking sand He lifted me.” Gabriel also wrote the tune for “Brighten the Corner Where You Are.”
stories.209: Johnson Oatman Jr. spent most of his working life in business in New Jersey, first in his father’s store and later in insurance. He wrote the words to this hymn a couple of years after he retired, and George Hugg wrote the tune the same year. Within a year it had been printed in 35 hymnbooks.
stories.210: In 1893, at the World’s Fair in Chicago, a preacher from London named Henry Varley told Daniel Whittle that he needed Christ not just every hour, as another hymn says, but every moment of the day. The thought stayed with Whittle, and he wrote this hymn. The words “moment by moment” come in every verse. His daughter May wrote the tune.
stories.212: Fanny Crosby, who was blind, had a friend named Phoebe Knapp who wrote music. Knapp played a new melody for her on the piano two or three times, then asked what the tune said. Crosby answered, “Blessed assurance, Jesus is mine!” The rest of the hymn followed within minutes.
stories.213: Daniel Whittle was a traveling preacher, and James McGranahan sang at his meetings. For more than ten years they worked together, and McGranahan wrote the tunes for many of Whittle’s hymns, this one too. It was first printed in 1883 in Gospel Hymns No. 4, a songbook of its day. Each verse begins with something the singer does not know. The refrain answers with Paul’s words in 2 Timothy 1:12: “I know whom I have believed.”
stories.214: Daniel Whittle wrote this hymn in 1883, and James McGranahan wrote its tune. It was first printed that year in Gospel Hymns No. 4, the same songbook as “I Know Not Why God’s Wondrous Grace.” Its first line is a promise God makes in Ezekiel 34:26: “there shall be showers of blessing.” In that chapter God speaks as a shepherd who will look for His scattered sheep and care for the hurt and the weak (Ezekiel 34:11–16).
stories.215: Knowles Shaw was a traveling preacher who also sang and wrote songs. He wrote this hymn in 1874. It grows from Psalm 126:5–6: “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.” A sheaf is a bundle of grain stalks tied together at harvest. The hymn is often called by its refrain, “Bringing in the Sheaves.”
stories.216: Ina Ogdon hoped to travel and speak at Chautauqua meetings, large summer gatherings for talks and teaching. Instead, her life kept her at home. This hymn grew out of what she came to believe there: the place where you already are is a place to serve. Charles Gabriel wrote its tune. It became the best-known song at the large meetings of the preacher Billy Sunday, where Homer Rodeheaver led the singing.
stories.218: Frank Davis was a music teacher and choir leader who lived in many places, from Maryland to Michigan. He wrote this hymn, words and tune, in 1880 on a steamboat in Chesapeake Bay. It was first printed the next year in a songbook called Bright Gems. Its refrain asks, “Gently down the stream of time, lead me, Saviour, all the way.” It is the one hymn he is remembered for.
stories.219: Lydia Baxter loved to talk with her friends about what the names in the Bible mean. The name that meant the most to her was Jesus. In Matthew 1:21 the angel tells Joseph to call Him Jesus, “for he shall save his people from their sins.” She wrote this hymn around 1870. William Doane wrote the tune for her words, and it was first printed in 1871 in Pure Gold, a songbook for Sunday schools that Doane made with Robert Lowry.
stories.220: Philip Bliss wrote both the words and the tune, and it was first printed in 1873 in a songbook for Sunday schools. It pictures a sailor leaving a wrecked ship for a lifeboat and rowing for shore as day breaks. Its second verse tells the sailor to watch “the Bright and Morning Star,” a name Jesus gives Himself in Revelation 22:16. In April 1912, people in one of the Titanic’s lifeboats sang it as they rowed.
stories.221: Isaac Watts first printed this in 1707 in his book Hymns and Spiritual Songs, under the heading “Godly sorrow arising from the sufferings of Christ.” On November 20, 1850, Fanny Crosby was at a church service when the people began to sing it. When they reached “Here, Lord, I give myself away,” she later wrote, her soul was “flooded with a celestial light.” She said that until then she had been trying to hold the world in one hand and the Lord in the other. The refrain was added in 1885 by Ralph Hudson, who also wrote this tune.
stories.222: On April 30, 1868, the composer William Doane came to Fanny Crosby’s home with a new melody. He said he had forty minutes before his train left for Cincinnati and asked if she could write words for it. She had the words in about twenty minutes. He wrote them down and caught his train.
stories.225: Eliza Hewitt lived all her life in and near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and cared a great deal about teaching children in Sunday school. John Sweney, a composer who also lived near Philadelphia, wrote the tune. This was one of the first songs they made together. It was first printed in 1887 in Glad Hallelujahs, a songbook Sweney helped put together. Each verse asks to know Jesus better, through His Word and His Spirit.
stories.226: This hymn pictures sailors on a ship in danger in a wild storm at night. A voice calls to them through the dark: “I’ll stand by until the morning, I’ve come to save you, do not fear.” To stand by is a sailor’s way of saying, “I will stay close and not leave you.” In the hymn, the one who calls is Jesus. Daniel Whittle wrote the words and James McGranahan the tune, and it was first printed in 1878 in Gospel Hymns No. 3.
stories.227: In 1906 Robert Harkness, a pianist traveling with a team that held large Christian meetings, met a young man in Toronto who had just come to faith. The young man was afraid he would not be able to hold on to it. Harkness wrote to his friend Ada Habershon in England and asked for songs that would help people like him. She sent back several, and among them were the words “He will hold me fast.” Harkness wrote the tune during a meeting in Philadelphia later that year.
stories.229: Elizabeth Prentiss wrote this prayer in 1856, during a hard time in her life. She wrote it quickly, in pencil, and did not finish the last verse. She kept it to herself for thirteen years, and in 1869 she showed it to her husband, George, a pastor. William Doane wrote its tune. She is also known for her book Stepping Heavenward, which came out that same year.
stories.230: Godfrey Thring wrote this hymn in 1886. Almost every line comes from Revelation, the last book of the Bible. It hears “harpers harping with their harps” (Revelation 14:2). It sees the holy city coming down from heaven “as a bride adorned” (Revelation 21:2), a city that needs no sun, because “the Lamb is the light thereof” (Revelation 21:23). Thring also wrote the Christmas hymn “From the Eastern Mountains.”
stories.231: Jane Borthwick wrote this as a poem called “O Lord, Thou Knowest!” It was printed in 1859 in her small book of poems, Thoughts for Thoughtful Hours. She often signed her poems “H. L. L.,” for Hymns from the Land of Luther, the book of German hymns she and her sister Sarah Findlater had put into English. This one is her own, not a translation. Each verse begins “Thou knowest,” and brings God her weariness, her past, and her present.
stories.238: Henry Williams Baker wrote this prayer for the first edition of Hymns Ancient and Modern, the hymnbook he helped put together, in 1861. It was meant to be sung in a time of war. Every verse ends the same way: “Give peace, O God, give peace again!” The words echo Psalm 29:11: “the LORD will bless his people with peace.”
